sentences.t:
Nealles mid gewealdum wyrmhord ābræc,
sylfes willum, sē ðe him sāre gesceōd,
ac for þrēanēdlan þ(ēow) nāthwylces
hæleða bearna heteswengeas flēah,
(ærnes) þearfa, ond ðǣr inne fealh,
secg synbysig.
sentences.l: Not at all with control the worm-hoard he broke into, by his own wishes, he who sorely harmed him, but for dire need the servant of some one or other of the sons of men fled hate-blows, needy of a house, and pushed in there, a man sin-troubled.
sentences.i: It was not of his own free will that he broke into the dragon’s hoard, the man who had done it such sore harm; he was the slave of some man or other, in dire need and running from savage beatings, a homeless wretch, and he forced his way in there, a man weighed down with guilt.
sentences.n: The subject is the man named last, ‘secg synbysig’, ‘a man sin-troubled’ (‘syn’ ‘crime’ + ‘bysig’ ‘troubled’; found only here). ‘mid gewealdum’ and ‘sylfes willum’ (‘by his own wishes’) both mean roughly ‘of his own accord’; the first, from ‘geweald’ ‘power’, is a guess at an idiom. ‘sē ðe him sāre gesceōd’ is ‘he who sorely harmed him’, ‘him’ being the dragon. ‘heteswengeas’ are ‘hate-blows’, beatings. ‘þ(ēow)’, ‘servant, slave’, is Grundtvig’s restoration of a lost word, where Kemble and Holthausen read ‘þ(egn)’, ‘thane’. ‘nāthwylces’ is ‘of some one or other’ (‘ne wāt hwylc’, ‘I know not which’), as at 2053. ‘(ærnes) þearfa’ is ‘needy of a house’; Zupitza finds ‘æ’ and ‘n’ almost certain. The manuscript has ‘horda’, a line break, then ‘cræft’ where Klaeber prints ‘hord ābræc’ (Kaluza’s correction; italic ‘b’, ‘c’). ‘fealh’ (italic ‘h’), from ‘feolan’ ‘force a way’, is Grein’s reading of a damaged ‘weall’.

sentences.t:
Sōna † mwatide
þæt : : : : : ðām gyst(e gryre)brōga stōd;
sentences.l: At once † mwatide that : : : : : to the guest (horror)-terror stood;
sentences.i: At once † … … terror and dread came over the guest;
sentences.n: ‘Sōna’ is ‘at once’. ‘mwatide’ cannot be read, and Klaeber marks it † as hopelessly corrupt; Thorpe, Schücking and Chambers emend to ‘inwlātode’ (‘looked in’), Holthausen to ‘hē wagode’, Sedgefield to ‘þæt geīode’, none certain, so I translate nothing from it. The colons are letters the manuscript no longer shows. What survives is ‘that … to the guest terror stood’: ‘ðām gyst(e)’ is a dative, ‘to the guest’, the unwelcome visitor in the barrow, and ‘gryrebrōga’ a nominative, ‘horror-terror’ (‘gryre’ ‘horror’ + ‘brōga’ ‘terror’), restored by Zupitza as ‘(e gryre)brōga’ after Grein’s earlier guess ‘gryre’. ‘stōd’ I take as ‘stood over him, came upon him’.

sentences.t:
hwæðre (earm)sceapen . . . . . . . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . sceapen
. . . . . . . . . . (þā hyne) se fǣr begeat.
sentences.l: Yet (wretchedly) shaped . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . shaped . . . . . . . . . . (when) the sudden peril seized (him).
sentences.i: Yet the wretched creature … … when the sudden terror seized him.
sentences.n: Nearly all of these three lines is lost, and Klaeber prints rows of dots. What survives is a skeleton: ‘hwæðre’ ‘yet’; ‘(earm)sceapen’ ‘wretchedly shaped’ (‘earm’ ‘wretched’ + ‘sceapen’, past participle of ‘scieppan’ ‘shape’; the same word is used of Grendel at 1351), with ‘earm’ restored; ‘sceapen’ again at the end of 2229; and ‘(þā hyne) se fǣr begeat’, ‘when the sudden peril overtook him’ (‘begietan’ ‘seize, overtake’, ‘fǣr’ ‘sudden danger’). Whom ‘hyne’ names is not shown; I take it to be the thief, because the lines on either side are about him, but that is inference from where the gap sits. The apparatus marks the start of the next manuscript leaf, folio 179b, at 2229.

sentences.t:
Sincfæt . . . . . þǣr wæs swylcra fela
in ðām eorð(hū)se ǣrgestrēona,
swā hȳ on gēardagum gumena nāthwylc,
eormenlāfe æðelan cynnes,
þanchycgende þǣr gehȳdde,
dēore māðmas.
sentences.l: Treasure-vessel . . . . . there was of such, many, in that earth-(ha)ll, of ancient treasures, as them in days of yore of men some one or other, a huge legacy of a noble race, thoughtfully there hid, dear treasures.
sentences.i: A treasure-cup … there; many such ancient treasures lay in that earth-hall, just as some man or other, in the days of long ago, had hidden them there with careful thought, the vast inheritance of a noble race, precious treasures.
sentences.n: ‘Sincfæt’, ‘treasure-vessel’ (‘sinc’ ‘treasure’ + ‘fæt’ ‘vessel’), is followed by a lost verb; Grein suggested ‘(sōhte)’, Heyne, Trautmann and Chambers ‘(geseah)’, Holthausen ‘(genōm)’ (‘sought, saw, took’), all guesses. Then ‘þǣr wæs swylcra fela … ǣrgestrēona’ is ‘there was of such many … of ancient treasures’ (‘fela’ takes the genitive; ‘ǣr-’ ‘former’). ‘eorð(hū)se’ is ‘earth-house’, the barrow, with ‘hū’ restored. In ‘swā hȳ … gehȳdde’ the object ‘hȳ’, ‘them’, is picked up by ‘eormenlāfe’ (‘huge legacy’) and ‘dēore māðmas’ (‘dear treasures’); the subject is ‘gumena nāthwylc’, ‘some one or other of men’, ‘þanchycgende’ ‘thinking carefully’ (‘þanc’ ‘thought’ + ‘hycgan’ ‘think’). ‘gēardagum’ is ‘in days of yore’, as in the first line of the Prologue; ‘æðelan cynnes’ is a genitive, ‘of noble race’.

sentences.t:
Ealle hīe dēað fornam
ǣrran mǣlum, ond sē ān ðā gēn
lēoda duguðe, sē ðǣr lengest hwearf,
weard winegeōmor wēnde þæs ylcan,
þæt hē lȳtel fæc longgestrēona
brūcan mōste.
sentences.l: All of them death took away at earlier times, and the one yet of the people’s veterans, who there longest went about, a guardian friend-sad, expected the same, that he a little while of the long-treasures might enjoy.
sentences.i: Death had taken all the rest in earlier times; and the one man still left of that people’s seasoned warriors, who had lived there longest, a guardian grieving for his friends, expected the same lot, that he would be allowed to enjoy those long-held treasures only for a little while.
sentences.n: ‘Ealle hīe dēað fornam’ is ‘death took all of them away’, ‘ǣrran mǣlum’ ‘at earlier times’ (dative). ‘sē ān ðā gēn’ is ‘the one still’ (Klaeber’s italic ‘e’ alters the manuscript’s ‘si’), with ‘lēoda duguðe’, ‘of the people’s tried retainers’. ‘weard’ I take as the noun ‘guardian’, in apposition to ‘sē’, with ‘winegeōmor’ ‘friend-sad’ (‘wine’ ‘friend’ + ‘geōmor’ ‘sad’). Zupitza reads the manuscript as first having ‘wearð’ ‘became’ (Chambers doubts the ‘ð’), and Thorpe, Holthausen and Sedgefield print that, giving ‘became friend-sad’; the reading is uncertain. ‘wēnde þæs ylcan’ is ‘expected the same’ (‘wēnan’ takes the genitive); the ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘lȳtel fæc’ ‘a little while’, ‘longgestrēona’ ‘of long-treasures’ (found only here; ‘treasures long held’ is a guess), a genitive after ‘brūcan’ ‘enjoy’, ‘mōste’ ‘might be allowed’.

sentences.t:
Beorh eallgearo
wunode on wonge wæterȳðum nēah,
nīwe be næsse, nearocræftum fæst;
þǣr on innan bær eorlgestrēona
hringa hyrde hordwyrðne dǣl,
fǣttan goldes, fēa worda cwæð:
sentences.l: A barrow all-ready stood on the plain near the water-waves, new by the headland, fast with narrow-crafts; there within bore the keeper of rings, of earl-treasures, a hoard-worthy share, of plated gold, few words said:
sentences.i: A barrow stood ready on the plain near the surging water, newly made beside the headland, secured by cunning workmanship; into it the keeper of the rings carried a share of the nobles’ treasure worth hoarding, plated gold, and spoke a few words:
sentences.n: ‘Beorh’ is the subject, ‘eallgearo’ ‘all-ready’ (Thorpe and Chambers print it as two words), ‘wunode’ ‘stood, was situated’; ‘wæterȳðum nēah’ is ‘near the water-waves’ (‘nēah’ takes the dative), the sea. ‘nīwe’ agrees with ‘beorh’, ‘new’, which I take as newly made. ‘nearocræftum fæst’ is ‘fast with narrow-crafts’ (‘nearo’ ‘tight, close’ + ‘cræft’), perhaps secured by close-fitting skilful work; that is a guess. ‘hringa hyrde’, ‘keeper of rings’, is a king’s title, here the last survivor. ‘hordwyrðne’ ‘worth hoarding’ is Klaeber’s alteration (italic ‘o’): the manuscript has ‘hard wyrðne’ (Zupitza wondering whether the ‘w’ of ‘wyrðne’ is an ‘f’), and Grein, Bouterwek and Bugge tried ‘hardfyrdne’, ‘hord byrhtne’ and ‘hordwynne’ in turn. ‘fǣttan goldes’ is ‘of plated gold’, the exact sense uncertain. ‘fēa worda cwæð’ is ‘spoke few words’; the colon opens his speech.

sentences.t:
‘Heald þū nū, hrūse, nū hæleð ne mōstan,
eorla ǣhte!
sentences.l: ‘Hold, you, now, earth, now that heroes might not, the earls’ possessions!
sentences.i: ‘Keep now, earth, what warriors were not allowed to keep, the possessions of earls!
sentences.n: This is the last survivor’s speech, begun at 2246. ‘Heald’ is the imperative singular of ‘healdan’ ‘hold, keep’, ‘hrūse’ a vocative, ‘earth’, and ‘eorla ǣhte’ the object, ‘the earls’ possessions’ (‘ǣht’ ‘property’), held back to the end of the sentence. ‘nū hæleð ne mōstan’ is ‘now that heroes might not’, ‘mōstan’ the past plural of ‘mōtan’ ‘be allowed’, with ‘hold’ understood. Klaeber’s italic ‘ō’ marks an alteration: the manuscript has ‘mæstan’, under which Zupitza thought ‘mostun’ (or ‘moston’) perhaps lay, and Chambers calls it ‘all very obscure’.

sentences.t:
Hwæt, hyt ǣr on ðē
gōde begēaton;
sentences.l: What! it earlier from you good ones got;
sentences.i: Listen! Good men won it from you long ago;
sentences.n: ‘Hwæt’ is the interjection ‘What!’, here a call for the earth’s attention. ‘hyt’ is ‘hit’, ‘it’, the treasure, object of ‘begēaton’, the plural past of ‘begietan’ ‘get, obtain’; its subject is ‘gōde’, ‘good (men)’, a noun. ‘ǣr’ is ‘formerly’. ‘on ðē’ is literally ‘on you’, and I read it as ‘from you’, the gold taken out of the ground; ‘on’ with the dative could also mean ‘in your keeping’, and I do not know which is meant.

sentences.t:
gūðdēað fornam,
feorhbealo frēcne fȳra gehwylcne
lēoda mīnra þāra ðe þis [līf] ofgeaf,
secga seledrēam.
sentences.l: war-death took away, life-bale, fierce, each of men, of my people, of those who gave up this [life], the hall-joy of men.
sentences.i: the death of battle has swept them off, a fierce destroyer of life, every one of my people who gave up this life, the hall-joy of men.
sentences.n: ‘gūðdēað’ ‘war-death’ and ‘feorhbealo’ ‘life-bale’ (‘feorh’ ‘life’ + ‘bealu’ ‘evil’) are two names for one killer, ‘frēcne’ ‘fierce’ an adjective or an adverb. The object is ‘gehwylcne’ ‘each’, with ‘fȳra’ ‘of men’ (‘fīras’, a poetic word) and ‘lēoda mīnra’ ‘of my people’, then ‘þāra ðe þis [līf] ofgeaf’ ‘of those who gave up this life’. Klaeber patches this line heavily. The manuscript has ‘fyrena’ for ‘fȳra’ (italic ‘a’) and ‘þana’ for ‘þāra’ (italic ‘ra’); ‘līf’ is Kemble’s addition (Holthausen would add ‘lēoht’, ‘light’); and where the manuscript has ‘gesawon’ Klaeber prints ‘secga’ (italic, Trautmann’s reading; Bugge read ‘geswǣfon seledrēamas’). ‘secga seledrēam’ is ‘of men hall-joy’, ‘seledrēam’ (‘sele’ ‘hall’ + ‘drēam’ ‘joy’); I take it in apposition to ‘līf’, life being men’s joy in the hall.

sentences.t:
Nāh, hwā sweord wege
oððe fe(o)r(mie) fǣted wǣge,
dryncfæt dēore; dug(uð) ellor s[c]eōc.
sentences.l: I own not who may bear a sword or polish the plated cup, the dear drink-vessel; the troop elsewhere departed.
sentences.i: I have no one to bear a sword or to burnish the plated cup, the precious drinking-vessel; the company of tried warriors has gone elsewhere.
sentences.n: ‘Nāh’ is ‘ne āh’, ‘I do not possess’, the pronoun unstated. ‘hwā … wege’ is ‘anyone who might bear’ (subjunctive of ‘wegan’), so ‘I have no one who …’. ‘fe(o)r(mie)’ is ‘polish, furbish’ (‘feormian’); the manuscript shows only ‘fe’ and an ‘r’ among other traces, and ‘feormie’ is Grein’s guess. ‘fǣted wǣge’ is ‘a plated cup’ (accusative) and ‘dryncfæt dēore’ ‘precious drink-vessel’ is in apposition. ‘dug(uð)’ is the company of tried retainers (Kemble’s restoration of the lost letters), ‘ellor’ ‘elsewhere’, a veiled way of saying they died. ‘s[c]eōc’, with Klaeber’s bracketed ‘c’, is the past of ‘scacan’ ‘go, depart’; the manuscript’s ‘seoc’ would be ‘sick’ and does not fit. Folio 180a begins at 2252.

sentences.t:
Sceal se hearda helm (hyr)stedgolde,
fǣtum befeallen;
sentences.l: The hard helmet shall, of ornament-gold, of plates, be bereft;
sentences.i: The hard helmet must be stripped of its ornamented gold, bereft of its plates;
sentences.n: ‘Sceal’ ‘shall, must’ with the participle ‘befeallen’ (‘befeallan’ ‘fall away from’, which takes the dative) gives ‘must be bereft’, ‘be’ left out. What it loses stands in the dative: ‘(hyr)stedgolde’, ‘ornament-gold’ (‘hyrsted’ ‘ornament’ + ‘gold’; Kock’s one-word form, where others print two words, with the first letters restored), and ‘fǣtum’, ‘plates’ or ‘plated work’, the dative plural of ‘fǣt’ ‘vessel’, a guess based on ‘fǣted’ ‘plated’ at 2253. ‘se hearda helm’ is ‘the hard helmet’.

sentences.t:
feormynd swefað,
þā ðe beadogrīman bȳwan sceoldon;
sentences.l: the polishers sleep, those who the battle-masks were to burnish;
sentences.i: the burnishers lie sleeping, whose task it was to polish the helmets;
sentences.n: ‘feormynd’ is the nominative plural of a noun from ‘feormian’ (2253), ‘those who polish’; Kemble, Grein and others print ‘feormend’ or ‘feormiend’, and Klaeber keeps the manuscript’s spelling. ‘swefað’ is ‘sleep’, meaning they are dead, like ‘ellor scēoc’ above. ‘þā ðe … sceoldon’ is ‘who were to’, with the infinitive ‘bȳwan’ ‘polish, adorn’. ‘beadogrīman’ is the accusative plural of ‘beadogrīma’, ‘battle-mask’ (‘beadu’ ‘battle’ + ‘grīma’ ‘mask’), a kenning for helmets; ‘grīma’ is ‘mask, visor’, and I do not know whether the word means the whole helmet or its face-guard.

sentences.t:
gē swylce sēo herepād, sīo æt hilde gebād
ofer borda gebræc bite īrena,
brosnað æfter beorne.
sentences.l: and likewise the war-coat, that which at battle endured, over the shields’ crash, the bite of irons, crumbles after the warrior.
sentences.i: And so with the mail-coat that endured in battle, amid the crash of shields, the bite of blades: it crumbles away now its warrior is gone.
sentences.n: ‘gē swylce’ is ‘and likewise’. ‘herepād’ is ‘war-coat’ (‘here’ ‘army, war’ + ‘pād’ ‘cloak, coat’), the mail-shirt, subject of ‘brosnað’ ‘crumbles, decays’; ‘sīo’ (a spelling of ‘sēo’) ‘that one’ opens a relative clause, ‘which’. ‘gebād’ is the past of ‘gebīdan’ ‘experience, live through’, with the accusative ‘bite’ and ‘īrena’, ‘of irons’, a genitive plural meaning swords. ‘ofer borda gebræc’ is ‘over/amid the crash of shields’ (‘gebræc’ ‘crashing’, ‘borda’ genitive plural), and ‘æfter beorne’ ‘after the warrior’, that is, after he has died.

sentences.t:
Ne mæg byrnan hring
æfter wīgfruman wīde fēran,
hæleðum be healfe.
sentences.l: Nor can the byrnie’s ring after the war-chief far travel, by the side of heroes.
sentences.i: Nor can the ring-mail travel far after its war-leader, at the side of heroes.
sentences.n: ‘Ne mæg’ is ‘cannot’, with the infinitive ‘fēran’ ‘travel’. ‘byrnan hring’ is ‘the byrnie’s ring’ (‘byrnan’ a genitive singular), the linked rings of the mail-shirt taken together. ‘æfter wīgfruman’ is ‘after the war-leader’ (‘wīg’ ‘war’ + ‘fruma’ ‘chief, first one’), which can mean ‘following him’ or ‘after his death’, and both come to the same thing. ‘wīde’ is ‘widely, far’; ‘hæleðum be healfe’ is ‘by the side of heroes’ (dative plural, ‘be healfe’ literally ‘by the half’, the side).

sentences.t:
Næs hearpan wyn,
gomen glēobēames, nē gōd hafoc
geond sæl swingeð, nē se swifta mearh
burhstede bēateð.
sentences.l: Was not the harp’s joy, mirth of the glee-wood, nor does a good hawk swing through the hall, nor does the swift steed beat the stronghold-place.
sentences.i: There is no joy of the harp now, no delight of the glee-wood; no good hawk sweeps through the hall, no swift steed beats the ground of the stronghold.
sentences.n: ‘Næs’ is the past, ‘was not’; Thorpe, Bugge and four editors print ‘nis’, ‘is not’, since the verbs that follow are present, but Klaeber keeps the manuscript, and I give the past in the literal version and a present in the idiomatic one. ‘hearpan wyn’ ‘the harp’s joy’ and ‘gomen glēobēames’ ‘mirth of the glee-wood’ are in apposition, ‘glēobēam’ (‘glēo’ ‘glee, music’ + ‘bēam’ ‘beam, wood’) a kenning for the harp. ‘swingeð’ is ‘swings, sweeps’, ‘geond sæl’ ‘through the hall’; ‘se swifta mearh’ is ‘the swift steed’ (‘mearh’, a poetic word for horse); ‘burhstede’ ‘stronghold-place’ I take to be the yard of a fortified dwelling, a guess; ‘bēateð’ ‘beats’, with hooves.

sentences.t:
Bealocwealm hafað
fela feorhcynna forð onsended!’
sentences.l: Baleful-death has many of the life-kinds forth sent!’
sentences.i: Baleful death has sent many a race of living men on their way!’
sentences.n: ‘Bealocwealm’ ‘baleful-death’ (‘bealu’ ‘evil’ + ‘cwealm’ ‘death, slaughter, plague’) is the subject; ‘hafað … onsended’ is ‘has sent away’ (‘onsendan’), ‘forð’ ‘forth’ (Zupitza reads the manuscript as ‘feorð’, meaning ‘forð’). ‘fela’ ‘many’ takes the genitive plural ‘feorhcynna’, ‘of life-kinds’ (‘feorh’ ‘life’ + ‘cynn’ ‘kind, race’), the races of living men. The closing quotation mark ends the survivor’s speech, begun at 2247.

sentences.t:
Swā giōmormōd giohðo mǣnde
ān æfter eallum, unblīðe hwe(arf)
dæges ond nihtes, oð ðæt dēaðes wylm
hrān æt heortan.
sentences.l: So sad-minded he bemoaned sorrow, one after all, joyless went about by day and by night, until death’s surge touched at the heart.
sentences.i: So, sad at heart, he mourned his sorrow, the only one left when all were gone, and wandered joyless by day and by night, until the surge of death touched his heart.
sentences.n: ‘giōmormōd’ ‘sad-minded’ (‘giōmor’ ‘sad’ + ‘mōd’ ‘mind’) agrees with an unstated ‘hē’; ‘giohðo’ ‘sorrow’ is the object of ‘mǣnde’ ‘lamented’ (‘mǣnan’). ‘ān æfter eallum’ is ‘alone after all (of them)’. ‘hwe(arf)’, ‘went about’, is a doubtful restoration: the manuscript has ‘hweop’ (Kemble) or something like it, ‘arf’ is Grein’s conjecture, and Schücking reads ‘wēop’, ‘wept’. ‘dæges ond nihtes’ is ‘by day and by night’ (genitives of time). ‘dēaðes wylm’ is ‘death’s surge’ (‘wylm’ ‘welling, surge’), and ‘hrān æt heortan’ ‘touched at the heart’ (‘hrīnan’, past ‘hrān’) is the poet’s way of saying he died. The narrator now takes up the story.

sentences.t:
Hordwynne fond
eald ūhtsceaða opene standan,
sē ðe byrnende biorgas sēceð,
nacod nīðdraca, nihtes flēogeð
fȳre befangen;
sentences.l: The old dawn-scather found hoard-joy standing open, he who, burning, seeks barrows, naked malice-dragon, by night flies, wrapped in fire;
sentences.i: The old dawn-raider found the joy of the hoard standing open, the naked, spiteful dragon who goes burning in search of barrows and flies by night wrapped in flame;
sentences.n: ‘fond’ takes ‘Hordwynne’, ‘hoard-joy’ (‘hord’ + ‘wynn’ ‘joy’), the treasure, as object, with ‘opene standan’ ‘standing open’; the subject follows the verb (the literal version puts it first, to keep the English clear): ‘eald ūhtsceaða’, ‘old dawn-scather’ (‘ūht’ ‘the hours before dawn’ + ‘sceaða’ ‘harmer, enemy’, as in ‘mānscaða’), the dragon. A relative clause describes him: ‘sē ðe byrnende biorgas sēceð’ ‘who burning seeks barrows’ (‘biorgas’ accusative plural of ‘beorh’), ‘nacod nīðdraca’ ‘naked malice-dragon’ (‘nīð’ ‘hate, malice’), ‘nihtes flēogeð’ ‘flies by night’, ‘fȳre befangen’ ‘wrapped in fire’ (‘befōn’ ‘enclose’). ‘nacod’ ‘naked’ is odd for a dragon in flames; I take it as ‘bare, unarmoured’, a guess, and ‘unsheathed’ is another possibility. The survivor is dead, and the dragon finds the hoard standing open.

sentences.t:
hyne foldbūend
(swīðe ondrǣ)da(ð).
sentences.l: him earth-dwellers (greatly dread).
sentences.i: Men on earth stand in great dread of him.
sentences.n: ‘hyne’ is ‘him’, the dragon, put first, object of ‘ondrǣdað’ ‘dread’ (which takes the accusative). The subject is ‘foldbūend’, ‘earth-dwellers’ (‘folde’ ‘earth’ + ‘būend’ ‘dwellers’), a poetic word for people, as in ‘foldbūende’ at 1355. Folio 180b begins at 2275 in the manuscript, and of ‘swīðe ondrǣdað’ only the letters ‘da’ survive; the rest is Zupitza’s restoration.

sentences.t:
Hē gesēcean sceall
(ho)r(d on) hrūsan, þǣr hē hǣðen gold
warað wintrum frōd; ne byð him wihte ðȳ sēl.
sentences.l: He shall seek out (the hoard in) the earth, where he heathen gold guards, wise in winters; not at all by that the better is it for him.
sentences.i: It is his nature to seek out the hoard in the earth, where he guards heathen gold, old and wise in years; yet he is not a whit the better for it.
sentences.n: ‘Hē gesēcean sceall’ is ‘he shall seek out’; ‘sceall’ can state what a creature is bound to do by its nature, which suits the dragon. The object is largely lost: Zupitza’s ‘(ho)r(d on)’ gives ‘hord on hrūsan’, ‘a hoard in the earth’, where Grein read ‘(hea)r(h on)’, ‘shrine on’. ‘þǣr hē hǣðen gold warað’ is ‘where he guards heathen gold’ (‘warian’ ‘guard’; ‘hǣðen’ ‘heathen’, the gold of the pagan dead), ‘wintrum frōd’ ‘wise in winters’. ‘ne byð him wihte ðȳ sēl’ is ‘it is not at all the better for him by that’ (‘wihte’ ‘in the least’, ‘ðȳ’ instrumental ‘by that’, ‘sēl’ ‘better’): the gold does him no good.

sentences.t:
Swā se ðēodsceaða þrēo hund wintra
hēold on hrūsan hordærna sum
ēacencræftig, oð ðæt hyne ān ābealch
mon on mōde;
sentences.l: So the people-scather three hundred of winters held in the earth one of the hoard-houses, hugely powerful, until one man angered him in mind;
sentences.i: So for three hundred winters the scourge of the people held one of those hoard-halls under the ground, enormously strong, until one man roused his anger;
sentences.n: ‘ðēodsceaða’ ‘people-scather’ (‘ðēod’ ‘people’ + ‘sceaða’) is the dragon again; ‘þrēo hund wintra’ ‘three hundred of winters’ is an accusative of time (‘hund’ takes the genitive plural). ‘hēold … hordærna sum’ is ‘held one of the hoard-houses’ (‘hordærn’ ‘hoard-house’, ‘sum’ ‘one of’), ‘on hrūsan’ ‘in the earth’; the manuscript has ‘hrusam’, and Thorkelin’s reading ‘hrūsan’ gives Klaeber’s italic ‘n’. ‘ēacencræftig’ is ‘hugely powerful’ (‘ēacen’ ‘huge, mighty’ + ‘cræftig’ ‘strong, skilled’), each part a little uncertain. ‘oð ðæt hyne ān ābealch mon on mōde’ is ‘until a certain man angered him in his mind’: ‘ābealch’ is the past of ‘ābelgan’ ‘anger’, with the accusative, and ‘ān … mon’ ‘one man’. The man is the thief.

sentences.t:
mandryhtne bær
fǣted wǣge, frioðowǣre bæd
hlāford sīnne.
sentences.l: to the liege-lord he bore a plated cup, for peace-pledge asked his lord.
sentences.i: he carried the plated cup to his liege-lord and begged his lord for terms of peace.
sentences.n: ‘mandryhtne’ is a dative, ‘to the liege-lord’ (‘man’ ‘man’ + ‘dryhten’ ‘lord’, the lord whose man one is), and ‘bær’ ‘bore’; ‘fǣted wǣge’ is ‘a plated cup’, as at 2253, presumably the cup taken from the hoard. ‘frioðowǣre’ is ‘peace-pledge’ (‘frioðu’ ‘peace’ + ‘wǣr’ ‘pledge, treaty’), in a form that could be genitive, dative or accusative singular; ‘biddan’ ‘ask’ takes the genitive or accusative for the thing asked, so it is one of those two, the person asked being the accusative ‘hlāford sīnne’, ‘his lord’. The poem says only that he asked for a pledge of peace; that the gift of the cup bought it is my reading of the order of events.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs hord rāsod,
onboren bēaga hord, bēne getīðad
fēasceaftum men; frēa scēawode
fīra fyrngeweorc forman sīðe. —
sentences.l: Then was the hoard explored, borne off the hoard of rings, a request granted to the destitute man; the lord looked at the men’s ancient-work for the first time. —
sentences.i: Then the hoard was searched out and carried off, that hoard of rings, and the poor man’s request was granted; his lord looked on the old work of men for the first time. —
sentences.n: ‘rāsod’ is a past participle of a verb found only here, taken as ‘explored, searched into’; ‘onboren’ is ‘borne off’ (‘onberan’), both with ‘wæs’. I take both as passive, the hoard looted of the cup and the rest, but the exact senses are guesses. Some editors doubt the repeated ‘hord’: Bugge reads ‘hearh’ and Holthausen and Sedgefield ‘hlǣw’ ‘barrow’ for the first, Bugge ‘dǣl’ and Cosijn ‘sum’ for the second. ‘bēne getīðad’ is ‘a request granted’ (‘bēne’ nominative, a variant of ‘bēn’; ‘getīðian’ ‘grant’), ‘fēasceaftum men’ ‘to the destitute man’ (dative; ‘fēa’ ‘few’ + ‘sceaft’ ‘creature, condition’), the thief. ‘frēa’ ‘lord’ is his master, who ‘scēawode’ ‘looked at’ ‘fīra fyrngeweorc’, ‘the ancient work of men’ (‘fyrn’ ‘old’ + ‘geweorc’), presumably the cup, ‘forman sīðe’ ‘for the first time’. The dash is Klaeber’s and marks a turn back to the dragon.

sentences.t: Þā se wyrm onwōc, wrōht wæs genīwad;
sentences.l: Then the worm awoke, strife was renewed;
sentences.i: Then the dragon woke, and the feud was begun again;
sentences.n: ‘onwōc’ is the past of ‘onwæcnan’ ‘awake’ (the same verb means ‘be born’ elsewhere), and ‘wyrm’ ‘worm, serpent, dragon’ (‘worm’ in the published fitt-13) is the word this part uses beside ‘draca’. ‘wrōht’ is ‘strife, enmity’, nominative, with ‘wæs genīwad’ ‘was renewed’ (‘genīwian’), a passive.

sentences.t:
stonc ðā æfter stāne, stearcheort onfand
fēondes fōtlāst; hē tō forð gestōp
dyrnan cræfte dracan hēafde nēah.
sentences.l: sniffed then along the stone, the stern-hearted one found the foe’s foot-track; he too far forth stepped, with secret craft, near the dragon’s head.
sentences.i: Then it sniffed along the rock, and the stern-hearted creature found the footprint of its enemy; for he had stepped too far forward, by secret craft, close to the dragon’s head.
sentences.n: ‘stonc’ is the past of ‘stincan’, which the lexica give both as ‘move quickly, spring’ and as ‘smell, sniff’. With ‘æfter stāne’, ‘along the stone’ (‘æfter’ with the dative), I take ‘sniffed’, because the dragon then finds a ‘fōtlāst’, ‘foot-track’; ‘darted’ is the other possibility, and this is a guess. ‘stearcheort’ is ‘stern-hearted’ (‘stearc’ ‘stern, hard’), the dragon, and ‘onfand’ ‘found out’. ‘fēondes’ ‘of the enemy’ is the thief. In ‘hē tō forð gestōp’, ‘he stepped too far forward’, the subject changes back to the thief; ‘dyrnan cræfte’ is ‘by secret craft’ (dative of means) and ‘dracan hēafde nēah’ ‘near the dragon’s head’, so he had gone close while it slept.

sentences.t:
Swā mæg unfǣge ēaðe gedīgan
wēan ond wrǣcsīð sē ðe Waldendes
hyldo gehealdeþ!
sentences.l: So can the not-doomed easily survive woe and exile-journey, he who the Wielder’s favour keeps!
sentences.i: So can a man who is not doomed come easily through misery and exile, if he keeps the Ruler’s favour!
sentences.n: ‘mæg’ ‘can’ (a statement, not a wish) with the infinitive ‘gedīgan’ ‘come through, survive’ takes the accusatives ‘wēan’ ‘woes’ and ‘wrǣcsīð’ ‘exile-journey’ (‘wrǣc’ ‘banishment, misery’ + ‘sīð’ ‘journey’). The subject is ‘unfǣge’, ‘one not doomed’ (‘fǣge’ ‘fated to die’, with ‘un-’), and ‘sē ðe … gehealdeþ’, ‘he who keeps’ (a general present), takes ‘Waldendes hyldo’, ‘the Wielder’s favour’; ‘Waldend’ is God, as at 1661. I take the aside to account for the thief’s escape: a man who is not fated to die gets through such dangers if God favours him.

sentences.l: The hoard-guard sought eagerly along the ground, wished to find the man who to him in sleep had sorely done;
sentences.i: The keeper of the hoard searched eagerly over the ground, wishing to find the man who had done him such harm as he slept;
sentences.n: ‘Hordweard’ ‘hoard-guard’ is the dragon; the word was used of a king at 1047. ‘sōhte … æfter grunde’ is ‘sought along the ground’ (‘æfter’ with the dative, as at 2288), ‘georne’ ‘eagerly’. ‘wolde guman findan’ is ‘wished to find the man’, ‘guman’ an accusative singular. ‘þone þe’ is ‘the one who’; ‘getēode’ is the past of ‘getēon’ ‘do, inflict’, with ‘him’ in the dative and ‘sāre’ ‘sorely’, the same adverb as at 2222. ‘on sweofote’ is ‘in sleep’. Some editors read the noun ‘sār’ ‘pain’ for ‘sāre’ (apparatus).

sentences.t:
hāt ond hrēohmōd hlǣw oft ymbehwearf
ealne ūtanweard;
sentences.l: hot and fierce-minded the barrow oft he went around, all of it outside;
sentences.i: Hot with rage and savage in mood he circled the barrow time and again, all around the outside of it;
sentences.n: ‘hāt ond hrēohmōd’ is ‘hot and fierce-minded’ (‘hāt’ ‘hot’, perhaps with fire or with fury; ‘hrēoh’ ‘rough, wild’ + ‘mōd’), agreeing with an unstated ‘hē’. ‘hlǣw’ is the accusative singular, ‘mound’; Klaeber’s italic ‘w’ marks his change, the manuscript having ‘hlæwū’ (Kemble and four editors print ‘hlǣw’, Grundtvig and others ‘hlǣw nū’). ‘ymbehwearf’ is ‘went around’ (‘ymbehweorfan’), ‘oft’ ‘often’, and ‘ealne ūtanweard’ ‘all of it, outward’, an accusative masculine; the manuscript has ‘ealne utanweardne’ and editors differ on the ending.

sentences.l: nor there any man in that waste — yet in war he rejoiced, in battle-work;
sentences.i: There was no man there in that wilderness — yet he took joy in war, in the work of battle;
sentences.n: The first clause has no verb: ‘nē ðǣr ǣnig mon on þǣre wēstenne’ is ‘nor any man there in that waste’, and one must supply ‘was’ or ‘was to be found’. The manuscript has only ‘ne’; Grein would add ‘wæs’, others ‘næs’, Sedgefield ‘wearð’, and Rieger assumes something lost after ‘wēstenne’, where Sedgefield supplies ‘wiht gesȳne’ and marks a second gap after ‘gefeh’, while Koeppel would strike out 2296b–2298a. The dash is Klaeber’s, marking the break in the sense. ‘hwæðre’ is ‘yet’; ‘wīges gefeh’ is ‘rejoiced in war’ (‘gefēon’ takes the genitive; ‘wīges’, italic, replaces the manuscript’s ‘hilde’, ‘battle’, which hardly changes the sense); ‘bea(du)[we] weorces’ is ‘of battle-work’, ‘beaduwe’ the genitive of ‘beadu’, partly restored and partly added by Klaeber (Holthausen and Sedgefield read ‘beaduweorces [georn]’, ‘eager for battle-work’).

sentences.t:
hwīlum on beorh æthwearf,
sincfæt sōhte;
sentences.l: at times into the barrow he turned back, sought the treasure-vessel;
sentences.i: now and then he turned back into the barrow, looking for the treasure-cup;
sentences.n: ‘hwīlum’ is ‘at times’ (a dative plural of ‘hwīl’ ‘while’ used as an adverb); ‘on beorh’ is ‘into the barrow’, with the accusative after a verb of motion; ‘æthwearf’ is the past of ‘æthweorfan’, ‘turn back, return’. ‘sincfæt’ is ‘treasure-vessel’, as at 2231, the object of ‘sōhte’ ‘sought’; the two clauses are joined with no ‘and’. The dragon is looking for the cup the thief took.

sentences.t:
hē þæt sōna onfand,
ðæt hæfde gumena sum goldes gefandod,
hēahgestrēona.
sentences.l: he that at once discovered, that one of men had of the gold made trial, of the high-treasures.
sentences.i: At once he found that some man had laid hands on the gold, the lofty treasures.
sentences.n: ‘hē þæt sōna onfand’ is ‘he at once found out that’, ‘þæt’ looking ahead to the clause. ‘gumena sum’ is ‘one of men’ (‘sum’ ‘a certain one’ with the genitive plural), and ‘hæfde … gefandod’ ‘had tried’, a perfect of ‘gefandian’ ‘put to the test, make trial of’, with the genitive ‘goldes’. I take it as ‘had meddled with the gold’, but the exact force of ‘gefandod’ is a guess. ‘hēahgestrēona’ is in apposition to ‘goldes’, ‘of high-treasures’ (‘hēah’ ‘high, noble’ + ‘gestrēon’ ‘treasure’), genitive plural.

sentences.t:
Hordweard onbād
earfoðlīce, oð ðæt ǣfen cwōm;
sentences.l: The hoard-guard waited with hardship, until evening came;
sentences.i: The keeper of the hoard waited, hard put to it, until evening came;
sentences.n: ‘onbād’ is the past of ‘onbīdan’ ‘wait’, ‘earfoðlīce’ an adverb, ‘with hardship’ (‘earfoð’ ‘hardship’ + ‘-līce’); I take it to mean he could hardly bear the delay, which is an inference from his rage. ‘oð ðæt ǣfen cwōm’ is ‘until evening came’ (‘cwōm’ the past of ‘cuman’). The semicolon is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
wæs ðā gebolgen beorges hyrde,
wolde se lāða līge forgyldan
drincfæt dȳre.
sentences.l: was then enraged the barrow’s keeper, wished the hateful one with flame to repay the dear drink-vessel.
sentences.i: Then the keeper of the barrow was swollen with anger; the hateful creature meant to repay the precious cup with fire.
sentences.n: ‘wæs ðā gebolgen’ is ‘was then enraged’ (‘gebolgen’ the participle of ‘gebelgan’), ‘beorges hyrde’ ‘the barrow’s keeper’ (‘hyrde’ ‘shepherd, guard’), the dragon. ‘wolde’ ‘wished to’ goes with ‘forgyldan’ ‘pay back, requite’, and ‘līge’ is ‘with flame’ (dative of means). ‘se lāða’ is ‘the hateful one’, an adjective used as a noun; Klaeber’s italic ‘se’ replaces the manuscript’s ‘fela ða’, a change due to Bugge. ‘drincfæt dȳre’ is ‘the dear drink-vessel’, the object (‘dȳre’ is a spelling of ‘dēore’, as at 2254): he means to avenge the cup with fire.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs dæg sceacen
wyrme on willan; nō on wealle læ[n]g
bīdan wolde, ac mid bǣle fōr,
fȳre gefȳsed.
sentences.l: Then was the day departed, to the worm’s wish; no longer on the wall would he wait, but with blaze went, by fire impelled.
sentences.i: Then the day was gone, as the dragon wished; he would not wait any longer by the wall, but set out in a blaze, driven on by fire.
sentences.n: ‘wæs … sceacen’ is ‘was gone’ (‘sceacen’ the participle of ‘scacan’ ‘depart’); ‘wyrme on willan’ is ‘to the worm’s will’, ‘as the dragon wished’. ‘nō … læng bīdan wolde’ is ‘would not wait any longer’; ‘læ[n]g’ has Klaeber’s bracketed ‘n’, the manuscript having ‘læg’, where Grundtvig reads ‘leng’. ‘on wealle’ is ‘at the wall’, the barrow’s, as I read it; the text does not say which wall. ‘bǣle’ is ‘with a blaze’ (‘bǣl’ ‘fire, pyre’), ‘fōr’ the past of ‘faran’ ‘went’, and ‘fȳre gefȳsed’ ‘by fire urged on’ (‘gefȳsan’ ‘impel’). ‘bǣl’ and ‘fȳr’ are two words for fire, and whether the second means his flame or his fury I do not know.

sentences.t:
Wæs se fruma egeslīc
lēodum on lande, swā hyt lungre wearð
on hyra sincgifan sāre geendod.
sentences.l: Was the beginning terrible to the people in the land, as it quickly was grievously ended on their treasure-giver.
sentences.i: That beginning was dreadful for the people of the land, as it came swiftly and bitterly to its end upon their lord, the giver of treasure.
sentences.n: ‘fruma’ ‘beginning’ is the subject of ‘wæs’, ‘egeslīc’ ‘terrible’ (‘ege’ ‘terror’ + ‘-līc’), and ‘lēodum on lande’ ‘to the people in the land’ (dative). ‘swā hyt lungre wearð … geendod’ is ‘as it was quickly brought to an end’ (‘wearð’ with a past participle makes a passive; ‘hyt’ is ‘hit’, the whole affair), ‘sāre’ ‘grievously’. ‘on hyra sincgifan’ is ‘on their treasure-giver’, the dative singular of ‘sincgifa’ (‘sinc’ ‘treasure’ + ‘gifa’ ‘giver’), the usual name for a king, here Beowulf, on whom the end falls. The narrator looks ahead: the dragon’s raid will cost the king his life. ‘swā’ may be ‘as’ or ‘so that’, with little difference.
